title: Booking a Trip in One Click
prompt: A travel site sells trips that combine a flight, a hotel and a rental car, each booked through a different partner's API, and then charges the customer. Design how a trip is booked so that a customer is never left with half a trip.
facts: About 50 trip bookings per second at peak
Measured failure rates: the car partner has no car for about 5% of requests, the hotel about 2%, the flight about 1%; the card charge fails for about 2%
Every partner accepts an idempotency key and offers a free cancellation within 24 hours of booking; the card provider can refund a charge
Requirement: the customer is never charged for an incomplete trip, never holds an incomplete trip, and learns the result within 30 seconds; the confirmation email cannot be taken back
Each partner call takes up to 3 seconds; the trip service saves its own data in its own database
scope: Changing or cancelling a trip later is out of scope

requirements: States that the customer must never be charged for or keep an incomplete trip, the 30-second result, and that the email cannot be undone
estimation: Compensations per second for the chosen step order, such as: with the car first, the 5% car failures (2.5 per second) need no compensation; with the flight first and the car last, each car failure needs 2 cancellations, about 5 per second
Or time: three partner calls and a charge at up to 3 seconds each is at most about 12 seconds, within 30
design: A saga: one local step per partner and for the charge, each with its compensation (cancel booking, refund), run by an orchestrator or by events
data: Step order with a reason: the most likely failure (the car) first, the charge after all bookings, the email last
Idempotency keys (the trip id) on every call and compensation; a saved trip state with an outbox so a crash does not lose the next step
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off or failure with its condition, such as: a partner call that times out may have booked, so the saga asks again with the same key before cancelling; a cancellation that fails is retried and then parked for a person; choreography is harder to follow than one orchestrator

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, orchestrated saga: the trip service saves the trip as pending with an outbox row, then books car → hotel → flight → charges the card → sends the email, each call with the trip id as idempotency key. A car failure (5%, 2.5 per second) needs no compensation; a hotel failure cancels the car; a flight failure cancels the hotel and car; a charge failure cancels all three. Worst case about 4 × 3 = 12 seconds, within 30. Trade-off: the trip service holds the workflow logic, one more part to run.

Design B, choreography: the trip service publishes "trip requested"; the car service books and publishes "car booked" or "car failed"; the hotel service reacts to "car booked", and so on, each saving its state and outbox in one local transaction. Each service listens for a later failure and cancels its own booking. Same step order and failure counts (car first, no compensation for 2.5 per second); same 12-second worst case. Trade-off: no single place shows the whole flow, which makes it harder to follow and debug as steps grow.

assumptions: Partners honor free cancellation within 24 hours
Partner failures are independent of each other
reference.design:
The trip service runs an orchestrated saga. It saves the trip as "pending" together with an outbox row, and its relay starts the first step.
Steps, in order: book the car (most likely to fail, 5%), book the hotel, book the flight, charge the card, then send the confirmation email, which cannot be taken back and so comes last. Every call carries the trip id as an idempotency key.
If a step fails, the service runs compensations in reverse for the steps that succeeded: a charge failure cancels the flight, hotel and car; a car failure needs nothing. With the car first, the 2.5 car failures per second need no cancellations, instead of about 5 per second if the car were booked last.
A call that times out is asked again with the same key before anything is cancelled. A cancellation that keeps failing goes to a dead-letter queue for a person.
Worst case: four calls at up to 3 seconds each, about 12 seconds, within 30.
alternatives: Choreography with events: no central orchestrator, but harder to follow
Rejected: charging the card first, because a later booking failure would need a refund for many trips

title: Paying Sellers When a Delivery Is Confirmed
prompt: On a marketplace, when a buyer confirms that an order arrived, three things must happen: the seller's balance in the Ledger service goes up, the buyer gets loyalty points in the Points service, and the buyer gets a receipt email. Design how the confirmation reaches the other services.
facts: About 200 delivery confirmations per second at peak
The Order service saves the confirmation in its own database; Ledger, Points and Email are separate services with their own databases
Requirement: once a confirmation is saved, the seller is credited and the points are added exactly once in effect, and the receipt is sent; nothing may be lost if a server crashes at any moment
Requirement: other services learn about a confirmation within 1 second
A broker with at-least-once delivery is available (SD 7); the email provider accepts an idempotency key
scope: Spreading the confirmation to other services
Disputes and refunds are out of scope

requirements: States that nothing may be lost after the confirmation is saved, that credits and points must take effect once, and the 1-second delay
estimation: Outbox load and delay, such as: 200 rows per second; a relay checking every 200 ms publishes about 40 rows per check, each within about 200 ms, within 1 second
Or explains that at-least-once delivery means some of the 200 per second can arrive twice after a relay crash
design: The Order service saves the confirmation and an outbox row in one local transaction; a relay publishes an event that Ledger, Points and Email each receive
data: Each consumer is idempotent: Ledger and Points record the order id with their change in one local transaction (a unique constraint), and Email passes the order id as the provider's idempotency key
The relay reads the outbox by polling or by change data capture, and marks rows as sent after publishing
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off or failure with its condition, such as: a relay crash after publishing repeats a message, which idempotent consumers absorb; polling adds load and delay, change data capture adds a tool to run; without the outbox a crash between saving and publishing loses the credit

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, outbox with a polling relay: the Order service writes the confirmation and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay polls every 200 ms, publishes about 40 rows per check to an "order delivered" topic and marks them sent. Ledger and Points each insert (order id, change) under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the credit, so a repeat fails harmlessly; Email uses the order id as the provider's key. Delay about 200 ms, within 1 second. Trade-off: polling every 200 ms adds a small steady load on the database.

Design B, outbox read by change data capture: the same outbox table, but a CDC tool reads new rows from the database's log and publishes them as they commit, usually within well under a second, without polling queries. Consumers are idempotent in the same way. Estimate: 200 events per second through one stream, well within a broker's capacity. Trade-off: a CDC tool is one more system to run and watch, in exchange for less database load and shorter delay.

assumptions: The broker keeps messages until consumers acknowledge them
Consumers acknowledge only after their local transaction commits
reference.design:
The Order service saves the confirmation and an outbox row in one local transaction, so either both exist or neither does.
A relay polls the outbox every 200 ms, publishes the new rows (about 40 per check at 200 per second) to an "order delivered" topic, and then marks them sent. Each event reaches consumers within about 200 ms, within 1 second.
If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it publishes those rows again. Ledger and Points therefore record the order id with their change in the same transaction, under a unique constraint: a second delivery fails the insert and changes nothing. Email passes the order id as the provider's idempotency key.
The result is at-least-once delivery with an exactly-once effect: every confirmation credits the seller and adds points once, and nothing is lost if a server crashes.
alternatives: Change data capture instead of polling: lower delay and load, one more tool
Rejected: saving the confirmation and then publishing in a separate step, because a crash in between loses the credit
